title: Epistolae
author: Sidonius Apollinaris
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0261.stoa0002.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.

passages.original: debent igitur vel aequaevi vel posteri nostri universatim ferventibus votis alterum te ut Demosthenem, alterum ut Tullium nunc statuis, si liceat, consecrare, nunc imaginibus, qui te docente formati institutique iam sinu in medio sic gentis invictae, quod tamen alienae, natalium vetustorum signa retinebunt: nam iam remotis gradibus dignitatum, per quas solebat ultimo a quoque summus quisque discerni, solum erit posthac nobilitatis indicium litteras nosse.
passages.english: Therefore our contemporaries or our descendants ought, all of them together, with fervent vows to consecrate you, as a second Demosthenes and a second Tullius, now with statues, if it were permitted, now with portraits. For those who have been formed and trained under your teaching will, even in the very midst of an unconquered nation, though a foreign one, retain the marks of ancient birth: for now that the grades of rank have been removed, by which every highest man used to be distinguished from every lowest, the only sign of nobility hereafter will be to know letters.
passages.notes: The clause 'sinu in medio sic gentis invictae, quod tamen alienae' is compressed; rendered as 'in the midst of an unconquered, though foreign, nation' (presumably the barbarian rulers). 'Tullius' is Cicero.

passages.original: Varronem logistoricum, sicut poposceras, et Eusebium chronographum misi, quorum si ad te lima pervenerit, si quid inter excubiales curas, utpote in castris, saltim sortito vacabis, poteris, postquam arma deterseris, ori quoque tuo loquendi robiginem summovere.
passages.english: I have sent Varro's Logistoricus, as you had asked, and Eusebius the chronographer. If the file of these reaches you, and if amid the cares of your watches, being as you are in camp, you have at least some chance leisure, you will be able, after you have wiped your weapons clean, to remove the rust of speaking from your mouth as well.
passages.notes: 'lima' (file, i.e. polish) is taken figuratively of these works' refining influence; the sense is somewhat uncertain. 'Logistoricum' may refer to Varro's Logistorici as a work title.

passages.original: Cum primum Burdigalam veni, litteras mihi tabellarius tuus obtulit plenas nectaris florum margaritarum, quibus silentium meum culpas et aliquos versuum meorum versibus poscis, qui tibi solent per musicum palati concavum tinnientes voce variata quasi tibiis multiforatilibus effundi. sed hoc tu munificentia regia satis abutens iam securus post munera facis, quia forsitan satiricum illud de satirico non recordaris: Satur est cum dicit Horatius euhoe.
passages.english: As soon as I came to Bordeaux, your letter-carrier delivered to me a letter full of the nectar of flowers and of pearls, in which you blame my silence and ask for some of my verses in exchange for your verses, which are accustomed to pour out from you through the musical vault of your palate, ringing with varied voice as if from many-holed pipes. But you do this, abusing royal generosity enough, now secure after receiving gifts, because perhaps you do not remember that satirical remark about the satirist: 'Horace is well fed when he cries euhoe.'
passages.notes: The quotation alludes to Juvenal 7.62 ('satur est cum dicit Horatius euhoe'), i.e. a poet sings best when well fed. 'abutens' is taken as 'making full use of'/'abusing'; the sense may be 'enjoying to the full'.
